claim: Thirty healthy participants (19 female) with mean age 24.7 ± 5.5 and self-reported BMI 23 ± 4.5 were included in Experiment 1.
source: The final sample consisted of n = 30 (19 female), mean age = 24.7 ± 5.5 and self-reported Body Mass Index (BMI) = 23 ± 4.5.
evidence: Directly stated demographic information about the sample in Experiment 1.

claim: Six amnesic patients and fourteen age-matched healthy controls were included in Experiment 2.
source: The final sample included n = 6 patients (one female) with amnesia (see Table 1 for demographic and neuropsychological data) and n = 14 (6 female) healthy controls matched for age (61.6 ± 10.5), education (15.7 ± 3.6), and verbal IQ (WAIS-III VIQ = 109.5 ± 10.2).
evidence: Directly stated demographic information about the sample in Experiment 2.

claim: Decision time in the value-based decision task was longer when choice options were closer in value.
source: RTs were longer for decisions between options for which the magnitude of ∆Value (|∆Value|) was smaller (Figure 2B, bottom).
evidence: Behavioral data showing relationship between RT and value difference, presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Choices and RT in both perceptual and value-based tasks were well described by drift diffusion models.
source: For both the perceptual and the value-based tasks, choices and RT were well described by drift diffusion models (Figure 2, solid lines).
evidence: Model fits to behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: BOLD activity in the hippocampus was more positively correlated with RT for value-based decisions than perceptual decisions.
source: BOLD activity in memory-related hippocampal regions was more positively correlated with RT for value-based decisions than perceptual decisions, consistent with our hypothesis that deliberation associated with resolving preference relies on memory-related hippocampal mechanisms.
evidence: fMRI analysis results showing differential hippocampal activation patterns between task types.

claim: The conjunction of RT effects and memory retrieval effects revealed significant shared BOLD activity in the hippocampus.
source: Critically, however, both showed significant effects in the hippocampus and, as shown in Figure 3 (and Figure 3—source data 2), the conjunction of these two effects revealed significant shared BOLD activity in the hippocampus.
evidence: Conjunction analysis results presented in Figure 3.

claim: Functional connectivity between the hippocampus and parietal cortex was greater for value-based decisions that took longer.
source: The strongest RT-dependent correlation was between the hippocampus and the parietal cortex (superior parietal lobule and precuneus), showing that functional connectivity between the hippocampus and parietal cortex was greater for value-based decisions that took longer (Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: PPI analysis results showing connectivity patterns, presented in Figure 4.

claim: Amnesic patients showed intact performance on perceptual decisions compared to healthy controls.
source: Patients took about the same amount of time as healthy controls to make a perceptual decision and there were no significant differences between the groups on accuracy (i.e. slopes of the choice function in Figure 5A, p=0.28) or RT (interaction between |color coherence| and group on RT, p=0.18; and main effect of group on RT, p=0.41).
evidence: Statistical comparison of patient and control performance on perceptual task, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Amnesic patients' choices on value-based decisions were more stochastic than those of healthy controls.
source: Although the amnesic patients' choices were clearly governed by ∆Value (red sigmoid function, Figure 5B top, simple effect of ΔValue on choices among amnesics, p<0.0001), their choices were more stochastic than those of the controls (flatter red sigmoid function, Figure 5B top, p=0.0008).
evidence: Behavioral data comparing choice consistency between patients and controls, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Amnesic patients were substantially slower than healthy controls on value-based decisions.
source: The more striking difference between the two groups was observed on RT during value-based decisions: the amnesic patients were substantially slower than healthy controls (Figure 5B bottom, p=0.0004).
evidence: RT data comparing patients and controls on value-based task, presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The slower RTs in amnesic patients were specific to the value-based compared to the perceptual decision task.
source: These slower RTs were specific to the value-based compared to the perceptual decision task (p=0.002 for the interaction between task type and group on RT).
evidence: Statistical test of interaction between task type and group on RT.

claim: Amnesic patients' RTs were less driven by subjective value ratings than healthy controls.
source: In addition, their RTs were less driven by subjective value ratings (flatter red curve in Figure 5B bottom). This difference between amnesic patients and healthy controls was statistically reliable (p=0.015, interaction between |ΔValue| and group on RT in a mixed effects linear regression, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the relationship between RT and value difference across groups, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Index of efficiency (IE) for value-based decisions was significantly lower in amnesic patients compared to controls.
source: For value-based decisions, IE was significantly lower in the amnesic patients compared to controls (Figure 5D, t11.84 = 4.2, p=0.0007, Welch's t-test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of efficiency index between groups, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Index of efficiency (IE) for perceptual decisions did not differ between amnesic patients and healthy controls.
source: For perceptual decisions, IE did not differ between amnesic patients and healthy controls (Figure 5C, t17.21 = 0.02, p=0.98, Welch's t-test)
evidence: Statistical comparison of efficiency index between groups for perceptual task, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The hippocampus is necessary for detailed and vivid prospection about future events.
source: First, extensive research demonstrates that the hippocampus is necessary for detailed and vivid prospection about future events (Addis and Schacter, 2008; Buckner, 2010; Hassabis et al., 2007; Klein et al., 2002; Race et al., 2011; Schacter et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampus contributes to relational encoding.
source: Second, and more broadly, the hippocampus is known to contribute to relational encoding (Cohen and Eichenbaum, 1993; Horner and Burgess, 2013), a term coined by Cohen and Eichenbaum (1993) to capture the essential role of the hippocampus across many cognitive processes that involve flexible comparison and association between distinct items and features (for reviews, see Barry and Maguire, 2019; Davachi, 2006; Eichenbaum, 2000; Eichenbaum, 2018; Konkel and Cohen, 2009; Palombo et al., 2015a; Shohamy and Turk-Browne, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research and reviews.

claim: The hippocampus is involved in decisions that explicitly depend on memory by requiring participants to use novel associations acquired in the experiment.
source: Recent studies have indeed linked hippocampal-based mnemonic processes to choice behavior by demonstrating that the hippocampus is involved in decisions that explicitly depend on memory by requiring participants to use novel associations acquired in the experiment (Barron et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2015; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Decisions take more time when choosing between options of similar value.
source: Even seemingly simple decisions such as those that involve preferences between a pair of familiar items take more time when they involve a choice between options of similar subjective value.
evidence: General observation about decision-making behavior.

claim: One explanation for why decisions take more time is that a commitment to a choice depends on the accumulation of evidence to a threshold.
source: One explanation for why such decisions take more time is that a commitment to a choice depends on the accumulation of evidence to a threshold, and when the evidence is weaker, more samples are required to reach such a threshold (Krajbich et al., 2010; Milosavljevic et al., 2010).
evidence: Theoretical explanation supported by citations.

claim: The hippocampus plays a key role in deliberation during value-based decisions by contributing to the comparison between items and the construction of internal samples of evidence.
source: Our central hypothesis is that the hippocampus plays a key role in this deliberation process, contributing to the comparison between items and the construction of internal samples of evidence bearing on the decision.
evidence: Central hypothesis of the study, to be tested experimentally.

claim: Prospection about future events is likely to guide value-based decisions because it allows a decision-maker to imagine the detailed outcome of each choice option.
source: This sort of prospection is likely to guide value-based decisions because it allows a decision-maker to imagine the detailed outcome of each choice option.
evidence: Logical inference connecting prospection to decision-making.

claim: The relational function of the hippocampus is thought to underlie its well-known role in episodic memory.
source: This relational function of the hippocampus is thought to underlie its well-known role in episodic memory, but the comparison of multiple dimensions of items and their relation to each other is also likely to help guide deliberation during decision making by supplying internal evidence about each option.
evidence: Statement about hippocampal function based on established knowledge and inference.

claim: If the hippocampus supports deliberation, then longer decision times should be related to more engagement of the hippocampus.
source: We reasoned that if the hippocampus supports deliberation, then longer decision times should be related to more engagement of the hippocampus.
evidence: Prediction based on the hypothesis, to be tested with fMRI.

claim: Amnesic patients may show differences in the way they deliberate about simple value-based decisions.
source: Although a choice between two familiar items is not typically thought to depend on the hippocampal memory system (Bartra et al., 2013; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Platt and Plassmann, 2014; Rangel and Clithero, 2014; Rangel et al., 2008), we reasoned that amnesic patients may nonetheless show differences in the way they deliberate about simple value-based decisions.
evidence: Prediction about patient behavior, contrasting with typical assumptions.

claim: Amnesic patients could take less time because their decisions involve less deliberation, or they could take more time because they try unsuccessfully to deliberate using evidence derived from relational mechanisms.
source: Amnesic patients could take less time because their decisions involve less deliberation, or they could take more time because they try unsuccessfully to deliberate using evidence derived from relational mechanisms.
evidence: Alternative predictions about patient behavior.

claim: The choice functions and range of RT were comparable in the perceptual and value-based tasks.
source: The choice functions and range of RT were comparable in the two tasks, as were the goodness of fits (for model parameter estimates, see Figure 2—source data 1; for individual participant fits, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of behavioral patterns across tasks, with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The full drift diffusion model produced a better fit compared to a model with no power law.
source: We considered simpler parameterizations of the model, but the full model presented here produced a better fit compared to a model with no power law (BIC = 19.45), and a better fit compared to a model with no power law and flat bounds (BIC = 168.45).
evidence: Model comparison statistics.

claim: The hippocampal BOLD activity might be related simply to the fact that the value-based decision task makes more demands on memory because it depends on identifying objects.
source: First, the hippocampal BOLD activity might be related simply to the fact that the value-based decision task makes more demands on memory because it depends on identifying objects.
evidence: Alternative explanation considered in control analyses.

claim: A main effect of value-based versus perceptual decisions reveals differences in BOLD activity along the ventral stream and in the medial temporal lobe, including the hippocampus.
source: Indeed, a main effect of value-based versus perceptual decisions reveals differences in BOLD activity along the ventral stream and in the medial temporal lobe, including the hippocampus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: fMRI results from control analysis, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: If object identification were the reason for the RT effects, one would expect to find only a main effect of task rather than a significant interaction between task and RT.
source: However, if object identification were the reason for the RT effects, one would expect to find only a main effect of task—that is, an overall difference between the two tasks regardless of deliberation time—rather than a significant interaction between task and RT.
evidence: Logical reasoning about expected pattern of results under alternative explanation.

claim: The observation of both a main effect of task and an interaction with RT suggests that differences in object recognition do not account for the finding in the hippocampus.
source: The observation of both a main effect of task and an interaction with RT suggests that differences in object recognition do not account for the finding in the hippocampus.
evidence: Inference from the pattern of results.

claim: The difference in the hippocampus is not related to differences in RT range between the two tasks.
source: This analysis revealed a similar result (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and Figure 3—source data 4), suggesting that the difference in the hippocampus is not related to differences in RT range.
evidence: Results from control analysis restricting RT range, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: RT-related activity in the hippocampus is greater for value-based than perceptual decisions, even after accounting for other correlates of RT.
source: This analysis again revealed RT-related activity in the hippocampus that is greater for value-based than perceptual decisions, even after accounting for other correlates of RT, both within an anatomical ROI of bilateral hippocampus and at a whole-brain corrected level (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—source datas 5–8).
evidence: Results from control analysis accounting for difficulty and other factors, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The conjunction between the RT effect and the memory map was found within the hippocampus ROI.
source: The conjunction between the RT effect and the memory map was again found within the hippocampus ROI (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: Conjunction analysis results in supplementary figure.

claim: The three-way conjunction between the differential effect of RT on BOLD and two independent meta-analysis maps shows overlap in the hippocampus.
source: The three-way conjunction between the differential effect of RT on BOLD and these two meta-analysis maps also shows overlap in the hippocampus (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Conjunction analysis with independent meta-analysis maps, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The amnesic patients did not show any obvious differences in their use of the value rating scale nor in the resulting range of ΔValues.
source: Notably, the patients did not show any obvious differences in their use of the value rating scale nor in the resulting range of ΔValues (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of rating distributions between groups, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The flatter choice function in patients is not explained by a difference in the use of the value rating scale but that the ∆Value derived from that scale had less purchase on their choices.
source: This implies that the flatter choice function is not explained by a difference in the use of the value rating scale but that the ∆Value derived from that scale had less purchase on their choices.
evidence: Inference from the comparison of rating distributions and choice behavior.

claim: Slower decisions in patients could be a sign of a speed-accuracy tradeoff favoring accuracy, but that does not appear to be the case.
source: In principle, slower decisions could be a sign of a speed-accuracy tradeoff favoring accuracy, but that does not appear to be the case, as the patients were both slower and less accurate (i.e. less consistent with initial subjective values) than the controls.
evidence: Reasoning about the pattern of results in patients.

claim: The index of efficiency captures the extent to which additional time was used to resolve sources of uncertainty that contribute to stochastic choice behavior.
source: The index captures the extent to which additional time was used to resolve sources of uncertainty that contribute to stochastic choice behavior.
evidence: Definition of the efficiency index measure.

claim: For perceptual decisions, the similar efficiency index between patients and controls is presumably because the uncertainty originates in the stimulus and its noisy representation by sensory neurons.
source: For perceptual decisions, IE did not differ between amnesic patients and healthy controls (Figure 5C, t17.21 = 0.02, p=0.98, Welch's t-test), presumably because the uncertainty originates in the stimulus and its noisy representation by sensory neurons (Britten et al., 1993; Mante et al., 2013; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998).
evidence: Interpretation of the efficiency index results for perceptual task, supported by citations.

claim: Whatever deliberative process the amnesics engaged in to reach their decisions, it was less efficient than the process used by the controls.
source: This implies that whatever deliberative process the amnesics engaged in to reach their decisions, it was less efficient than the process used by the controls.
evidence: Inference from the efficiency index comparison for value-based decisions.

claim: While there was no support for the heuristic model in healthy controls, at least one feature of the RTs from the amnesic patients is consistent with this model.
source: While we found no support for this model in healthy controls (DDM performs better than this heuristic model, BIC = 537.5), at least one feature of the RTs from the amnesic patients is consistent with this model (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Model comparison results and qualitative assessment, with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The measurable differences between amnesics and controls in accuracy and RT may be related to a fundamental difference in how the amnesics resolve value-based preferences.
source: This observation does not provide definitive support for the heuristic above, but it does suggest that the measurable differences between amnesics and controls in accuracy and RT may be related to a fundamental difference in how the amnesics resolve value-based preferences.
evidence: Interpretation of the heuristic model analysis results.

claim: The findings link the timing of value-based decisions about highly familiar options to the hippocampus.
source: Together, these findings link the timing of value-based decisions about highly familiar options to the hippocampus.
evidence: Summary statement of the main findings from both experiments.

claim: Value-based decisions between highly familiar choice options are typically assumed to rely on subjective value.
source: Value-based decisions between highly familiar choice options are typically assumed to rely on subjective value (Levy and Glimcher, 2012; Rangel et al., 2008; Tversky and Kahneman, 1986).
evidence: Statement about typical assumptions in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Value signals are thought to be supported by the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC).
source: Such value signals are thought to be supported by the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC, Camille et al., 2011; Fellows, 2016; Fellows and Farah, 2007; Levy and Glimcher, 2011; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).
evidence: Statement about neural basis of value signals, supported by citations.

claim: Even when choosing between options that differ greatly in their subjective value, such choices involve a comparison of the values by way of taking both options, their relation, and their predicted value, into account.
source: Yet, even when choosing between options that differ greatly in their subjective value, such choices involve a comparison of the values by way of taking both options, their relation, and their predicted value, into account (Houston et al., 1999; Tversky, 1972; Voigt et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about decision processes, supported by citations.

claim: Resolving the choice between two options with similar value likely requires the generation of additional information—that is, evidence—to resolve the indecision.
source: Resolving the choice between two options with similar value likely requires the generation of additional information—that is, evidence—to resolve the indecision.
evidence: Theoretical reasoning about decision processes.

claim: This evidence must come from internal sources and might involve multiple dimensions of comparisons between the options.
source: This evidence must come from internal sources and might involve multiple dimensions of comparisons between the options.
evidence: Theoretical reasoning about the nature of evidence in value-based decisions.

claim: The role of the hippocampus in value-based decisions is almost certainly more nuanced than memory retrieval of the value associated with each of the items.
source: Our findings suggest that the role of the hippocampus in value-based decisions is almost certainly more nuanced than memory retrieval of the value associated with each of the items.
evidence: Interpretation of the findings in relation to hippocampal function.

claim: Prior work suggests that simple object-value associations do not depend on the hippocampus.
source: Prior work suggests that simple object-value associations do not depend on the hippocampus (Neubert et al., 2015; Reynolds et al., 2001; Rudebeck et al., 2008; Rushworth et al., 2011; Schultz et al., 1997; Vo et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about prior research findings, supported by citations.

claim: It is not obvious why a simple associative memory process would account for longer deliberation times.
source: Moreover, it is not obvious why a simple associative memory process would account for longer deliberation times.
evidence: Logical reasoning about the limitations of simple associative memory explanations.

claim: The hippocampus contributes to deliberative processes during decision making by supporting the construction of value from internal evidence and engagement in the comparison between the options.
source: Instead, we propose that the hippocampus contributes to deliberative processes during decision making. Specifically, we propose that deliberation may be served by the construction of value from internal evidence and engagement in the comparison between the options.
evidence: Proposed mechanism for hippocampal contribution to decision-making.

claim: Deliberation may involve evaluation of alternatives and prospection about future hypothetical experiences.
source: Such a process is likely to also involve evaluation of alternatives and prospection about future hypothetical experiences.
evidence: Extension of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Prior work suggests that evaluation of alternatives and prospection are likely to engage the hippocampus.
source: Prior work suggests that all these processes are likely to engage the hippocampus (Barron et al., 2013; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2001; Schacter et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement about prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The findings extend recent results demonstrating a role for the hippocampus in value-based decisions under conditions in which value information has been experimentally manipulated to depend on retrieval of new associative memories.
source: Our findings extend recent results demonstrating a role for the hippocampus in value-based decisions under conditions in which value information has been experimentally manipulated to depend on retrieval of new associative memories (Barron et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2015; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).
evidence: Positioning of current findings in relation to prior work, with citations.

claim: Recent work has characterized sampling processes during value-based decisions that are reliant on memory.
source: Recent work has also characterized sampling processes during value-based decisions that are reliant on memory (Bornstein and Norman, 2017; Bornstein et al., 2017; Duncan and Shohamy, 2016).
evidence: Statement about recent research, supported by citations.

claim: The study builds on prior findings to implicate the hippocampus functionally and establish a causal role for the hippocampus in decisions about familiar options for which value is known.
source: Our study builds on these findings to implicate the hippocampus functionally and establish a causal role for the hippocampus in decisions about familiar options for which value is known.
evidence: Summary of the contribution of the current study.

claim: One open question is whether the hippocampal role varies as a function of the nature of the items under deliberation.
source: One open question is whether this role varies as a function of the nature of the items under deliberation.
evidence: Identification of an open question for future research.

claim: Natural versus packaged items may vary in the extent to which perceptual features reveal their value.
source: For example, natural versus packaged items may vary in the extent to which perceptual features reveal their value; the color of an apple is revealing of its sweetness, the color of a package of chocolate perhaps less so.
evidence: Example illustrating potential variation in item properties.

claim: All value-based decisions depend on the transformation of external perceptual input to internal estimates of subjective value bearing on the relative desirability of the items.
source: But ultimately, all such decisions depend on the transformation of external perceptual input to internal estimates of subjective value bearing on the relative desirability of the items.
evidence: General statement about the nature of value-based decisions.

claim: It is this deliberative process—beyond the simple item-value association—that the hippocampus contributes to.
source: It is this deliberative process—beyond the simple item-value association—that we posit the hippocampus contributes to.
evidence: Clarification of the proposed hippocampal contribution.

claim: A similar pattern of less consistent decisions and longer decision times has been shown recently in healthy older adults with mild memory deficits.
source: A similar pattern has been shown recently in healthy older adults with mild memory deficits (Levin et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about related findings in another population, with citation.

claim: It is unlikely that amnesic patients simply cannot remember the value of the items, as their choices are not arbitrary.
source: As noted earlier, it is unlikely that amnesic patients simply cannot remember the value of the items, as their choices are not arbitrary.
evidence: Inference from the pattern of patient behavior.

claim: The patients may be relying on degraded value signals that are coarser than those in controls.
source: This suggests that the patients may be relying on degraded value signals that are coarser than those in controls.
evidence: Interpretation of patient behavior.

claim: Studies of simple valuation have described general valence signals in neurons in orbitofrontal cortex, striatum, amygdala, and anterior cingulate cortex that could potentially drive choices.
source: Studies of simple valuation have described general valence signals in neurons in orbitofrontal cortex, striatum, amygdala, and anterior cingulate cortex that could potentially drive these choices (Figure 3—figure supplement 5; Hayden et al., 2009; Hikosaka et al., 2014; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Platt and Plassmann, 2014; Saez et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about neural basis of valuation, supported by citations and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Patients with vmPFC damage show greater stochasticity in their choices but do not display the slowing in RT during deliberation seen in patients with amnesia due to hippocampal damage.
source: Interestingly, patients with vmPFC damage also show greater stochasticity in their choices (Camille et al., 2011; Fellows and Farah, 2007; Pelletier and Fellows, 2019), but do not display the slowing in RT during deliberation that we see in the patients with amnesia due to hippocampal damage.
evidence: Comparison with findings from patients with different lesions, supported by citations.

claim: The findings point to possible complementary roles for the hippocampus and the vmPFC in guiding value-based decisions.
source: This finding and others (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Wikenheiser et al., 2017; Wimmer and Büchel, 2016), point to possible complementary roles for the hippocampus and the vmPFC in guiding value-based decisions (also see, McCormick et al., 2018), with the hippocampus possibly supporting evidence-based construction of value and deliberation (Weilbächer and Gluth, 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in relation to broader neural systems, supported by citations.

claim: If patients resolve their choices by accessing a simpler form of value representation, then the question is why they take such a long time to reach decisions.
source: If patients resolve their choices by accessing a simpler form of value representation, then why do they take such a long time to reach decisions?
evidence: Question raised by the pattern of patient results.

claim: The long decision times in patients reflect their attempt to engage hippocampal relational mechanisms and their failure to do so.
source: We propose that this reflects the patients' attempt to engage hippocampal relational mechanisms and their failure to do so.
evidence: Proposed explanation for patient behavior.

claim: For perceptual decisions, a sequence of samples of blue and yellow dots can be converted by the visual system to samples of evidence.
source: In the perceptual task, a sequence of samples of blue and yellow dots can be converted by the visual system to samples of evidence by spatially integrating blue or yellow (or the difference) across the stimulus aperture in sampling epochs governed by the temporal resolution of the color system, which is slower than the frame rate of the display.
evidence: Description of the evidence sampling process in perceptual decisions.

claim: The samples in perceptual decisions are independent, identically distributed random values drawn from a distribution with an expectation determined by the stimulus strength and a variance governed by the stochastic properties of the stimulus and neurons.
source: The samples are independent, identically distributed random values drawn from a distribution with an expectation (i.e. mean) determined by the stimulus strength and a variance governed by the stochastic properties of the stimulus and the neurons that represent blue, yellow or blue minus yellow.
evidence: Description of the statistical properties of evidence samples in perceptual decisions.

claim: Similar logic has been applied to value-based decisions, but the analogy breaks down at the nature of the evidence samples.
source: As mentioned earlier, similar logic has been applied to value-based decisions (Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Milosavljevic et al., 2010; Polanía et al., 2015), but the analogy breaks down at the nature of the evidence samples.
evidence: Statement about limitations of applying perceptual decision models to value-based decisions, with citations.

claim: The stimulus in value-based decisions provides only one sample of the objects, and there is no reason to think that the brain would then generate a sequence of independent samples of ∆Value.
source: However, the stimulus provides only one sample of the objects, and there is no reason to think that the brain would then generate a sequence of independent samples of ∆Value (Shadlen and Shohamy, 2016).
evidence: Reasoning about the nature of evidence in value-based decisions, with citation.

claim: The comparison itself triggers constructive thought processes to provide samples of evidence that bear on evaluation of the items along a dimension.
source: Instead, we reason that the comparison itself triggers constructive thought processes to provide samples of evidence that bear on evaluation of the items along a dimension.
evidence: Proposed mechanism for evidence generation in value-based decisions.

claim: It is hard to imagine integrating samples of ∆Value along different dimensions, although it is possible if they were converted to some common currency.
source: It is hard to imagine integrating these samples of ∆Value along different dimensions, although it is possible if they were converted to some common currency (e.g. Kira et al., 2015).
evidence: Discussion of potential mechanisms, with citation.

claim: It seems at least equally likely that each sample leads to a new internal estimate of preference, only to terminate if such a sample provides a sufficiently compelling preference.
source: It seems at least equally likely that each sample leads to a new internal estimate of preference, only to terminate if such a sample provides a sufficiently compelling preference.
evidence: Alternative proposed mechanism for value-based decisions.

claim: Although the alternative process involves no integration, the drift diffusion model can be fit to such a process well enough to render these alternatives indistinguishable.
source: Although such a process involves no integration, the drift diffusion model can be fit to such a process well enough to render these alternatives indistinguishable (Ditterich, 2006).
evidence: Statement about model fitting limitations, with citation.

claim: The longer RTs in the amnesic patients stem from their continued effort to generate evidence to resolve the comparison.
source: On this view, the longer RTs in the amnesic patients stem from their continued effort to generate evidence to resolve the comparison.
evidence: Interpretation of patient behavior based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The greater stochasticity in patients' choices possibly stems from the fact that they may fail to generate evidence and ultimately fall back on a more rudimentary and noisier form of value representation to guide their choices.
source: Accordingly, the greater stochasticity in their choices possibly stems from the fact that they may fail to generate such evidence and ultimately fall back on a more rudimentary and noisier form of value representation to guide their choices.
evidence: Interpretation of patient choice behavior based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: One limitation of the present study is the inability to identify the specific hippocampal-based process that guides deliberation.
source: One limitation of the present study is that we are unable to identify the specific hippocampal-based process that guides deliberation.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitation.

claim: The study can only observe the manifestation of the hippocampal process in RT and its associated changes in hippocampal BOLD activity or the effect of hippocampal damage.
source: We can only observe the manifestation of the process in RT and its associated changes in hippocampal BOLD activity or the effect of hippocampal damage.
evidence: Description of what can be observed with current methods.

claim: The study deliberately avoided any possibility of biasing participants to adopt a memory-based strategy to resolve value preference.
source: In this study, we deliberately avoided any possibility of biasing participants to adopt a memory-based strategy to resolve value preference, as we were interested in testing whether memory spontaneously contributed to such decisions without instruction or guidance.
evidence: Explanation of experimental design choice.

claim: The idea that memory supports construction of evidence to guide value-based decisions offers new insights to understanding how decisions are made.
source: The idea that memory supports construction of evidence to guide value-based decisions offers new insights to our understanding of how decisions are made, as well as the role of the hippocampus in guiding behavior.
evidence: Statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The finding that the hippocampus supports deliberation between choice options with similar subjective value addresses Buridan's paradox.
source: The finding that the hippocampus supports deliberation between choice options with similar subjective value addresses a challenge that has long puzzled economists and philosophers (often referred to as Buridan's paradox, Chislenko, 2016; Sorensen, 2004).
evidence: Statement about the theoretical significance of the findings, with citations.

claim: By linking the hippocampus to choice behavior, this finding highlights the pervasive and broad role of the hippocampus in guiding actions and decisions.
source: By linking the hippocampus to choice behavior, this finding also highlights the pervasive and broad role of the hippocampus in guiding actions and decisions.
evidence: Statement about the broader implications for understanding hippocampal function.

claim: Research on the hippocampus has typically focused on its role in supporting the formation of conscious, declarative memories for episodes of one's life.
source: Research on the hippocampus has typically focused on its role in supporting the formation of conscious, declarative memories for episodes of one's life.
evidence: Statement about traditional view of hippocampal function.

claim: The current findings add to a growing shift in the view of hippocampal function, suggesting that the hippocampus may serve a more general purpose in guiding behavior by providing behaviorally relevant input about relational associations to implicitly guide actions and decisions.
source: The current findings add to a growing shift in this point of view, suggesting that the hippocampus may serve a more general purpose in guiding behavior by providing behaviorally relevant input about relational associations to implicitly guide actions and decisions (Chun and Phelps, 1999; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2001; Hannula et al., 2007; Olsen et al., 2016; Palombo et al., 2015a; Ryan et al., 2000; Schapiro et al., 2014; Shohamy and Turk-Browne, 2013; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).
evidence: Statement about the contribution to evolving understanding of hippocampal function, supported by citations.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at Columbia University.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at Columbia University and all scan participants provided signed informed consent before taking part in the study.
evidence: Statement about ethical approval.

claim: All patients and age-matched healthy participants provided informed consent in accordance with the Institutional Review Boards at Boston University and the VA Boston Healthcare System.
source: All patients and age-matched healthy participants provided informed consent in accordance with the Institutional Review Boards at Boston University and the VA Boston Healthcare System.
evidence: Statement about ethical approval for patient study.

claim: All patients presented with severe anterograde and retrograde amnesia.
source: All patients presented with severe anterograde and retrograde amnesia.
evidence: Clinical characterization of patient sample.

claim: Patients had lower than normal memory scores (two to three standard deviations below normal as measured by WMS-III), but were largely within normal range for measures of working memory and verbal aptitude.
source: Patients had lower than normal memory scores (two to three standard deviations below normal as measured by WMS-III, Table 1), but were largely within normal range for measures of working memory and verbal aptitude.
evidence: Neuropsychological characterization of patients, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Within the MTL, two patients (P03, P06) had lesions restricted to the hippocampus, while three patients had volume loss extending outside of the hippocampus (P01, P02, P05).
source: Within the MTL, two patients (P03, P06) had lesions restricted to the hippocampus, while three patients had volume loss extending outside of the hippocampus (P01, P02, P05).
evidence: Description of lesion extent in patient sample.

claim: For four of the patients (P02, P03, P05, P06), it was possible to determine that the lesion overlapped with the peak of hippocampal activation in the fMRI study.
source: For four of the patients (P02, P03, P05, P06), it was possible to determine that the lesion overlapped with the peak of hippocampal activation in the fMRI study.
evidence: Comparison of patient lesions with fMRI activation.

claim: Participants were trained to criterion on the perceptual color dots task, defined as 80% or higher accuracy over the last four blocks of 10 trials.
source: They were trained on the perceptual color dots task (details below), received feedback (correct/incorrect) on each trial during training, and were trained to criterion, defined as 80% or higher accuracy over the last four blocks of 10 trials.
evidence: Description of training procedure.

claim: The auction followed Becker-Degroot-Marschak (BDM) rules.
source: The auction followed Becker-Degroot-Marschak (BDM) rules (Becker et al., 1964).
evidence: Description of auction procedure, with citation.

claim: The auction procedure allowed obtaining a measure of willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each of 60 appetitive food items per participant.
source: This auction procedure allowed us to obtain a measure of willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each of 60 appetitive food items per participant (Plassmann et al., 2007).
evidence: Description of the purpose of the auction, with citation.

claim: Participants were given a chance to revise their bids to account for adjustments and scaling effects that can occur after participants experience the full food stimulus set.
source: After participants placed bids on all 60 items, they were given a chance to revise their bids to account for adjustments and scaling effects that can occur after participants experience the full food stimulus set.
evidence: Description of bid revision procedure and its rationale.

claim: The 60 food items were rank-ordered based on WTPs obtained during the auction, and 150 unique pairs were formed such that the difference in WTP between the two items in a pair (i.e. ∆Value) varied.
source: The 60 food items were rank-ordered based on WTPs obtained during the auction, and 150 unique pairs made up from the 60 items were formed such that the difference in WTP between the two items in a pair (i.e. ∆Value) varied.
evidence: Description of how food pairs were constructed for the choice task.

claim: Each of the 60 food items appeared in five different pairs during the food choice task.
source: Each of the 60 items appeared in five different pairs.
evidence: Description of stimulus presentation frequency.

claim: Participants were told that they would be given the chosen food on a single randomly selected trial to eat.
source: Participants were told that they would be given the chosen food on a single randomly selected trial to eat.
evidence: Description of incentive structure.

claim: Participants were presented with 210 trials total in the food choice task, split into three 70-trial scan runs.
source: Participants were presented with 210 trials total, split into three 70-trial scan runs.
evidence: Description of task structure.

claim: In the color dots task, dots were presented at random locations within a central circular aperture and replaced in each video frame (60 Hz) by new dots.
source: Dots were presented at random locations within a central circular aperture (diameter 5 cm) and replaced in each video frame (60 Hz) by new dots (density 16.7 dots•cm−2•s−1) at new random positions.
evidence: Description of stimulus properties in perceptual task.

claim: Participants were presented with a total of 210 trials in the color dots task, split into three scan runs of 70 trials each.
source: Participants were presented with a total of 210 trials, split into three scan runs of 70 trials each.
evidence: Description of task structure.

claim: In the memory recognition task, participants were presented with 100 objects they had rated during session one as well as 100 new objects, randomly intermixed.
source: Participants were presented with the 100 objects they had rated during session one as well as 100 new objects, randomly intermixed, one object at a time in the middle of the screen.
evidence: Description of memory test structure.

claim: The 200 trials in the memory recognition task were split into four scan runs of 50 trials each.
source: The 200 trials were split into four scan runs of 50 trials (approximately 5 min) each.
evidence: Description of task structure.

claim: The value-based decision task in Experiment 2 differed from Experiment 1 in that it used a preference rating scale rather than a BDM auction.
source: Rather than a BDM auction, participants indicated their pre-experimental preferences for 30 food items using a preference rating scale.
evidence: Description of methodological difference between experiments.

claim: Foods that a participant did not recognize or misnamed were excluded from analysis in Experiment 2.
source: Participants were asked to name the food item on the screen before rating it. Foods that a participant did not recognize or misnamed were excluded from analysis.
evidence: Description of exclusion criteria to ensure familiarity.

claim: Participants in Experiment 2 were given 3.5 s rather than 2.5 s to make a choice in the value-based task.
source: Participants were given 3.5 s rather than 2.5 s to make a choice.
evidence: Description of methodological difference between experiments.

claim: Participants in Experiment 2 were not asked to fast before the experiment and did not receive a snack at the end of the experiment.
source: Participants were not asked to fast before the experiment and did not receive a snack at the end of the experiment based on their choice on a randomly selected trial.
evidence: Description of methodological difference between experiments.

claim: Participants in Experiment 2 continued to receive correct/incorrect feedback throughout the entire perceptual decision task.
source: participants continued to receive correct/incorrect feedback throughout the entire task
evidence: Description of methodological difference between experiments.

claim: Imaging data were acquired on a 3 T GE MR750 MRI scanner with a 32-channel head coil.
source: Imaging data were acquired on a 3 T GE MR750 MRI scanner with a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: Description of MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Functional data were acquired using a T2*-weighted echo planar imaging sequence with TR = 2 s, TE = 22 ms, FA = 70°, FOV = 192 mm, acquisition matrix of 96 × 96.
source: Functional data were acquired using a T2*-weighted echo planar imaging sequence (repetition time (TR) = 2 s, echo time (TE) = 22 ms, flip angle (FA) = 70°, field of view (FOV) = 192 mm, acquisition matrix of 96 × 96).
evidence: Description of functional imaging parameters.

claim: Forty oblique axial slices were acquired with a 2 mm in-plane resolution positioned along the anterior commissure-posterior commissure line and spaced 3 mm to achieve full brain coverage.
source: Forty oblique axial slices were acquired with a 2 mm in-plane resolution positioned along the anterior commissure-posterior commissure line and spaced 3 mm to achieve full brain coverage.
evidence: Description of slice acquisition parameters.

claim: Raw imaging data in DICOM format were converted to NIFTI format and preprocessed through a standard preprocessing pipeline using the FSL package version 5.
source: Raw imaging data in DICOM format were converted to NIFTI format and preprocessed through a standard preprocessing pipeline using the FSL package version 5 (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: Description of preprocessing software and procedures, with citation.

claim: Spatial smoothing was performed using a Gaussian kernel with a full-width half maximum (FWHM) of 5 mm.
source: Spatial smoothing was performed using a Gaussian kernel with a full-width half maximum (FWHM) of 5 mm.
evidence: Description of preprocessing parameter.

claim: Data and design matrix were high-pass filtered using a Gaussian-weighted least-squares straight line fit with a cutoff period of 100 s.
source: Data and design matrix were high-pass filtered using a Gaussian-weighted least-squares straight line fit with a cutoff period of 100 s.
evidence: Description of preprocessing parameter.

claim: The functional volumes for each participant and run were registered to the high resolution T1-weighted structural volume using a boundary-based registration method implemented in FSL5.
source: The functional volumes for each participant and run were registered to the high resolution T1-weighted structural volume using a boundary-based registration method implemented in FSL5 (BBR, Greve and Fischl, 2009).
evidence: Description of registration procedure, with citation.

claim: The T1-weighted image was registered to the MNI152 2 mm template using a linear registration implemented in FLIRT (12 degrees of freedom).
source: The T1-weighted image was then registered to the MNI152 2 mm template using a linear registration implemented in FLIRT (12 degrees of freedom).
evidence: Description of registration to standard space.

claim: The drift diffusion model assumes that choice and RT are linked by a common mechanism of evidence accumulation, which stops when a decision variable reaches one of two bounds.
source: The model assumes that choice and RT are linked by a common mechanism of evidence accumulation, which stops when a decision variable reaches one of two bounds.
evidence: Description of the drift diffusion model.

claim: Time-varying decision bounds were used to account for potential differences in RT between correct and error trials.
source: We used time-varying decision bounds to account for potential differences in RT between correct and error trials.
evidence: Description of model feature.

claim: The model was fit to maximize the joint likelihood of choice and RT of each trial.
source: The model was fit to maximize the joint likelihood of choice and RT of each trial.
evidence: Description of model fitting procedure.

claim: The likelihood of the parameters given the data from each trial was obtained by numerically solving the Fokker-Planck (FP) equation describing the dynamics of the drift-diffusion process.
source: The likelihood of the parameters given the data from each trial was obtained by numerically solving the Fokker-Planck (FP) equation describing the dynamics of the drift-diffusion process.
evidence: Description of model fitting method.

claim: The parameter optimization was performed using the Nelder-Mead Simplex Method to minimize the negative log-likelihood of the parameters given the choice and RT data.
source: The parameter optimization was performed using the Nelder-Mead Simplex Method (Lagarias et al., 1998) to minimize the negative log-likelihood of the parameters given the choice and RT data.
evidence: Description of optimization method, with citation.

claim: The best fit parameters were taken from one hundred fits using random starting points to ensure that the optimization search did not get stuck in a local minimum.
source: We took the best fit parameters from one hundred fits using random starting points to ensure that the optimization search did not get stuck in a local minimum.
evidence: Description of procedure to avoid local minima in optimization.

claim: The heuristic model posits that RT is not governed by ∆Value but by whether the comparison is trivial or non-trivial.
source: The model posits that RT is not governed by ∆Value but by whether the comparison is trivial or non-trivial.
evidence: Description of alternative model prediction.

claim: The qualitative prediction of the heuristic model is refuted in healthy participants but not in amnesic patients.
source: This qualitative prediction is refuted in panels (A and B) (healthy participants, p<0.005), but not in panel (C) (amnesic patients; p=0.29).
evidence: Statistical test of heuristic model prediction, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The heuristic model does not outperform the drift diffusion model for any of the groups.
source: The heuristic model does not outperform the drift diffusion model for any of the groups, but it highlights a qualitative distinction between the amnesic patients and the other healthy groups.
evidence: Model comparison conclusion.

claim: A PPI analysis was used to identify brain regions with activity that covaried in an RT-dependent manner with the activity of hippocampal seed voxels.
source: We used a psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analysis to identify brain regions with activity that covaried in an RT-dependent manner with the activity of hippocampal 'seed' voxels—that is those that exhibited RT-dependent activation on the value-based decision task and memory-related activation on the memory localizer task.
evidence: Description of PPI analysis method.

claim: The PPI regressor was created by deconvolving the seed to obtain an estimated neural signal during value-based decisions using SPM's deconvolution algorithm.
source: The PPI regressor was created by deconvolving the seed to obtain an estimated neural signal during value-based decisions using SPM's deconvolution algorithm (Gitelman et al., 2003), calculating the interaction with the task in the neural domain and then reconvolving to create the final regressor.
evidence: Description of PPI regressor construction, with citation.

claim: The group-level analysis was performed using FSL's mixed effects modeling tool FLAME1.
source: The group-level analysis was performed using FSL's mixed effects modeling tool FLAME1 (Beckmann et al., 2003).
evidence: Description of group-level analysis method, with citation.

claim: For whole-brain correction, cluster-based Gaussian random field correction for multiple comparisons was used, with an uncorrected cluster-forming threshold of z = 2.3 and corrected extent threshold of p<0.05.
source: for whole-brain correction, we used cluster-based Gaussian random field correction for multiple comparisons, with an uncorrected cluster-forming threshold of z = 2.3 and corrected extent threshold of p<0.05.
evidence: Description of multiple comparisons correction method.

claim: For small volume correction, voxel-based Gaussian random field theory-based maximum height thresholding was used with a voxel-level corrected threshold of p<0.05 within a 3D mask of a region of interest.
source: For small volume correction, we used a voxel-based Gaussian random field theory-based maximum height thresholding with a voxel-level corrected threshold of p<0.05 within a 3D mask of a region of interest.
evidence: Description of small volume correction method.
